newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Mark unsettled, Euro shares revive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mark unsettled, Euro shares revive.

text.p: The mark put on a shaky performance on Tuesday, suffering from market concern that a single European currency to replace it could fail to match its strength.
French shares, however, added to Monday's surprise gains after the Socialist-led victory in the weekend parliamentary elections.

"The fundamentals are good and we have to stay calm," said Jean Laurent Bruel, fund manager at Banque Sifas. "Just because there's a change in government, companies aren't going to stop making profits. We have to seize opportunities."

Elsewhere, the London stock market was unsettled by fears of higher interest rates but the Frankfurt bourse advanced as the German monetary authorities patched up a spat over the value of gold reserves.
The Bonn government backed down in a row with the Bundesbank over plans to revalue the central bank's assets to help Germany qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

This climbdown led analysts to question again how Germany could prevent more countries making the grade for the euro currency -- which would potentially weaken it -- if Bonn continued to struggle to meet the strict economic qualification criteria itself.
Asked whether Germany would meet the EMU criteria in 1997 despite the lack of a windfall from the Bundesbank, Finance Minister Theo Waigel insisted: "We will manage it in 1997."
But Bonn now faces another 10 billion mark ($5.8 billion) hole to fill in its 1997 budget.
"The question is how will Germany meet the three percent target," said Julian Jessop, an economist at Nikko Europe.
Under the European Union's Maastricht treaty, the reference level for budget deficits to qualify for EMU is three percent of gross domestic product.
"A soft EMU, with Italy in at the start, is foremost in the market's mind at the moment," Jessop added.
The mark slipped to around 982.75 lire in late business from 983.50 a day earlier.
The Swedish crown also gained further against the soft mark after news that Sweden, as expected by markets, will not be on the EMU starting line in 1999.
The mark traded around 4.4845 Swedish crowns, down from 4.4985 before the afternoon announcement and 4.5130 late on Monday.
The French franc, which had hit a low for the year of 3.3860 per mark after the election results, traded around 3.3715 against the unsettled German currency.

Market perceptions that the left's victory in the French parliamentary poll could lead to broad membership of a euro currency from the planned 1999 start had helped the dollar hit a morning high of 1.7330 marks.
Socialist Elisabeth Guigou, tipped for office in the new Paris government, said her party would respect the start date for EMU.

Traders said if a broadly-based euro was launched on time without really tough measures to back it, rather than a delay which could prompt funds to flood back into the mark, it would be good news for the dollar.

"We know the Socialists want to go ahead on time but we know they're not so committed to actually meeting the criteria themselves -- that's underpinning the dollar," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at SGST.
"If the German government and its central bank find it hard to agree with each other, then it's safer to stick your money in dollars," added Eddie Tofpik, trader at MeesPierson Derivatives.
But some currency analysts said the market could be underestimating the chances of an EMU delay.
The dollar, meanwhile, was also underpinned by market speculation that key U.S. jobs data for May, due on Friday, could be strong, boosting prospects for higher interest rates next month.
French stocks ended in the plus column for the third consecutive session as investors cheered encouraging remarks by the new Socialist leaders and a drop in U.S. leading economic indicators.
But brokers cautioned that trading would be volatile ahead of details of the new government's plans and its composition.

Gains on Wall Street and higher bond prices helped British shares pare their losses by the close after jitters over higher interest rates and next month's first budget for the new British Labour government.
On Wall Street, the Dow Jones industrial average reversed early losses to show a gain of around 30 points or 0.4 percent towards the end of the New York morning after Monday's loss of 41.64 points.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted around 1.7275 marks and 116.10 yen, compared with 1.7266 and 116.63 in late European trading on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE 100 index ended down 5.0 points or 0.11 percent at 4,557.8, well above its low of 4,524.2.
PARIS - The CAC 40 closed up 23.04 points or 0.89 percent at 2,624.49.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended floor trade up 20.12 points or 0.56 percent at 3,625.74. The IBIS DAX was up 59.19 points or 1.65 percent at 3,655.59 in after-hours electronic trading.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold ended London trading lower at $342.85 an ounce after an afternoon fix of $343.55 and previous London close of $344.05.
